p.title: What does this unit measure?

items.text: litre (L)
items.why: 1 L = 10⁻³ m³ = 1000 cm³

items.text: cubic centimetre (cm³)
items.why: 1 cm³ = 10⁻⁶ m³

items.text: ångström (Å)
items.why: 1 Å = 10⁻¹⁰ m

items.text: fermi (fm)
items.why: 1 fm = 10⁻¹⁵ m — used for nuclear sizes

items.text: light year (ly)
items.why: Not a time! It is the distance light travels in one year, ≈ 9.46 × 10¹⁵ m

items.text: astronomical unit (AU)
items.why: Mean Earth–Sun distance, ≈ 1.496 × 10¹¹ m

items.text: electron volt (eV)
items.why: Energy gained by an electron through 1 V: 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J

items.text: erg
items.why: CGS unit of energy: 1 J = 10⁷ erg

items.text: joule (J)
items.why: SI unit of energy: 1 J = 1 N m

p.challenge: Sort each unit by the quantity it measures. Careful with the light year!

p.title: Order of magnitude (a × 10ᵇ: a ≤ 5 → b, a > 5 → b + 1)
p.challenge: Use the NCERT rule to give the order of magnitude of each quantity.
x = 0.1t³ (x in m, t in s). Slide h → 0 to watch Δx/Δt approach the tangent slope dx/dt, then drag P to the instant when the instantaneous velocity is 1.2 m s⁻¹.
x = 2.5 + 5t², so v = dx/dt = 10t. Drag P to the moment when v = 20 m s⁻¹. Watch the slope grow by the same amount every second: a = d²x/dt² = 10 m s⁻².
A scooter's velocity changes from 5 m s⁻¹ to 25 m s⁻¹ in 4 s. Set u and a = Δv/Δt so your graphs match the dashed ones. Notice the x–t curve bends upward when a > 0.

A ball is thrown up at 20 m s⁻¹ (g = 10 m s⁻²): v = 20 − 10t. Area under the v–t graph = displacement. Keep a = 0 and drag b to the top of the flight, where the ball is 20 m up. Then drag b to 4 s: why is the area zero there?
A car at 10 m s⁻¹ accelerates at 2 m s⁻² for 5 s. Set u and a, press Go and check x = v₀t + ½at² = 75 m. Read v = v₀ + at off the v–t graph at the end.
A particle has x₀ = 5 m, v₀ = 3 m s⁻¹, a = 2 m s⁻². Write x = x₀ + v₀t + ½at² as y = ax² + bx + c (x-axis = t) and set the sliders. Then read its position at t = 4 s from the table.
Free fall from rest: set u = 0 and a = g = 9.8 m s⁻² and press Go. Each 1-second dot gap grows 4.9, 14.7, 24.5, 34.3 m: Galileo's 1 : 3 : 5 : 7. The stone should fall 78.4 m in 4 s.
Forces of 5 N (A) and 3 N (B) act on a body. 5 kg + 3 kg is always 8 kg, but forces add as vectors. Turn B (keep it 3 N) to get the SMALLEST possible resultant, 2 N. Where is the largest?
Head-to-tail addition: A = (3, 0) m and B = (1, 2) m are fixed. Drag C so that the resultant R = A + B + C ends at (6 m, 4 m). What are C’s components?
Rain falls vertically at 8 m s⁻¹, then a wind blows from west to east at 6 m s⁻¹ (you face east). Stand still and tilt the umbrella so you stay dry: tan θ = v_w / v_r.
A force of 5 N acts at 30° above the +x axis. Predict Fₓ = F cos θ and F_y = F sin θ, then set F and check. Turn F to 90° and 180°: what happens to each component?
A boat moves at 8 km h⁻¹ due north in still water; the river flows east at 6 km h⁻¹ (x = east, y = north). Drag the boat's velocity, then read R = √(A² + B²) and its direction from north.

r = 3t î + 2t² ĵ traces the path y = 2x²/9. Velocity is always along the tangent, so its slope is v_y / vₓ. Find the point where the tangent slope is 4/3: that is t = 1 s, where v = 3î + 4ĵ m s⁻¹ (speed 5 m s⁻¹).
r = 2t î + t³ ĵ gives vₓ = 2 m s⁻¹ (constant) and v_y = 3t². The slope of the v_y–t graph is a_y. Find the instant when a_y = 6 m s⁻² — then a = 6ĵ m s⁻², since aₓ = 0.
v₀ = 4î m s⁻¹ and a = 2ĵ m s⁻², from the origin. At t = 3 s the v₀t part is 12î m (drawn). Work out ½at² and drag it into place so that r = v₀t + ½at². How far is the particle from O?
With g = 10 m s⁻², a ball projected at 20 m s⁻¹ and 30° is at (17.3 m, 5 m) after 1 s: the top of its path. Launch a ball through that ring. Watch vₓ stay constant while v_y shrinks to zero.
R = u² sin 2θ / g. Keep u = 20 m s⁻¹ (g = 10 m s⁻²) and land on the flag at 20 m with TWO different angles. Compare their heights and flight times.
A stone is thrown horizontally (θ = 0) from a 45 m cliff (g = 10 m s⁻²). It falls for t = √(2h/g) = 3 s. Choose the speed that makes it land 30 m from the base.

A stone goes anticlockwise round a circle at a steady 4 m s⁻¹. v₁ is its velocity at the right-most point. Drag v₂ to its velocity a quarter-turn later (top of the circle, still 4 m s⁻¹). Δv = v₂ − v₁ points towards the centre!

Aristotle said a push is needed to KEEP a body moving. Get the 10 kg cart sliding, then lower your push until it moves at constant speed (a = 0). Your push now only balances friction: net force is zero.
Galileo's inclines: with no friction, a ball rolling down one slope climbs the other to the same height. Release the ball so it just reaches the flag at 1 m on the far side.
A 4 kg block on frictionless ice. Use F = ma to choose the net force that gives a = 5 m s⁻², then push. Starting from rest, what is its velocity after 3 s?
A 0.15 kg ball arrives at 20 m s⁻¹ (p₁ = 3 kg m s⁻¹) and is hit straight back at 20 m s⁻¹. Drag p₂, then read the impulse Δp = p₂ − p₁. If contact lasts 0.01 s, what is the average force?

A shell moving along x has momentum 6 kg m s⁻¹ just before it explodes. One fragment flies off with p₁ = (4î + 3ĵ) kg m s⁻¹. Internal forces can't change the total: drag p₂ so that p₁ + p₂ = 6î kg m s⁻¹.

A 4 kg mass hangs on a string (W = 40 N, g = 10 m s⁻²) and is pulled aside by a horizontal F = 30 N (1 grid unit = 10 N). In equilibrium the forces close into a triangle: drag the tension T so that W + F + T = 0. Read T and tan θ with the vertical.

On an incline the normal reaction N balances the part of the weight pressing into the surface, mg cos φ. For a 2 kg block (g = 10 m s⁻²), tilt the incline until N = mg cos φ = 17.3 N. Which force pulls it down the slope?

A 10 kg box on a floor with μ_s = 0.5 and μ_k = 0.4 (g = 10 m s⁻²). Push with 30 N: what friction acts? Find the smallest push that starts it sliding, and watch friction drop to μ_k N = 40 N once it moves.

A woman pushes a trunk with 100 N for the first 10 m; then her push falls linearly to 50 N over the next 10 m. Work = area under the F–x graph. Keep a = 0 and drag b until she has done 1750 J of work.
Only gravity (a conservative force) does work, so K + V stays constant: mgH = ½mv². Choose the release height H so the ball passes the bottom at 6 m s⁻¹ (g = 10 m s⁻²). Predict H first.
A 1000 kg car hits a spring buffer (k = 16000 N m⁻¹) at 4 m s⁻¹, so the spring must store ½mv² = 8000 J. Work done = triangle under F = kx = ½kx². Drag b to the maximum compression.

A billiard ball at 5 m s⁻¹ (along x) hits an identical ball at rest elastically and goes off at 4 m s⁻¹, 37° above x. Equal masses, so momentum conservation needs v₁ + v₂ = u. Drag v₂ into place, then check the angle between v₁ and v₂.
Masses 1 kg at (0, 0), 1 kg at (4 m, 0) and 2 kg at (0, 4 m). Work out X = Σmᵢxᵢ/M and Y = Σmᵢyᵢ/M, then plot the centre of mass.

A see-saw pivoted at its centre (g = 10 m s⁻²): a 30 kg child (300 N) sits 2 m from the pivot. The other child weighs 400 N. Move them until load × load arm = effort × effort arm. Where must the 40 kg child sit?

A wheel starts from rest with α = 2 rad s⁻², so ω = 2t. Angular displacement θ is the area under the ω–t graph (θ = ω₀t + ½αt²). Drag b to the time when θ = 25 rad. About how many revolutions is that?
g = GM/R². A planet with twice the Earth's mass and twice its radius has g = G(2M)/(2R)² = g/2. Weigh the same mass on Earth and on Planet X: the weight halves, the mass doesn't.
A wire stretches by 2 mm under a final load of 100 N (F grows linearly with ΔL). The stored elastic energy is the area under the F–ΔL line, ½FΔL. Drag b until the energy is 100 N mm = 0.1 J.
A 60 kg girl (weight 600 N, g = 10 m s⁻²) stands on one heel of area 1 cm². Make the pressure P = F/A = 6 × 10⁶ Pa, then try a flat shoe and a snowshoe with the same force.
Heat ice at −10 °C steadily until it is steam. Watch the thermometer stop at 0 °C and at 100 °C while the state changes: the heat goes into changing the state (latent heat), not the temperature.

p.title: Wien's law: λ_m T = b = 2.9 × 10⁻³ m K
p.challenge: Use T = b / λ_m to match each peak wavelength to the temperature of the black body. Hotter → shorter λ_m.
A body cools in a 20 °C room: T = 20 + 70e^(−0.1t). Newton's law of cooling: dT/dt = −k(T − T_s), here k = 0.1 min⁻¹. Find the moment it is cooling at 5 °C per minute. What is T − T_s then?

p.title: First law: ΔQ = ΔU + ΔW (ΔW = work done BY the gas)

items.text: Absorbs 500 J, does 200 J of work
Absorbs 100 J, does 300 J of work
Absorbs 200 J, does 200 J of work
Insulated (ΔQ = 0), gas does 150 J of work
items.why: ΔU = 0 − 150 = −150 J: adiabatic expansion cools the gas

items.text: Insulated, 150 J of work done ON the gas
50 J of heat supplied, volume fixed
items.why: No work at constant volume: ΔU = ΔQ = +50 J

items.text: Loses 80 J of heat, volume fixed
items.why: ΔU = ΔQ = −80 J

items.text: Ideal gas expands isothermally
items.why: U of an ideal gas depends only on T, so ΔU = 0 (ΔQ = ΔW)

items.text: Gas completes a full cycle
items.why: It returns to its initial state, so ΔU = 0

p.challenge: Use the NCERT sign convention to decide whether the internal energy rises, falls or stays the same.
1 mol of ideal gas at 300 K expands isothermally: PV = μRT = 8.31 × 300 ≈ 2493 J (V in litres, P in kPa). Work done = area under the isotherm. Drag b until W = μRT ln(V₂/V₁) ≈ 1728 J. What is V₂/V₁?

p.title: Allowed by the second law?

items.text: Engine takes 1000 J from a hot reservoir, does 1000 J of work, rejects nothing
items.why: Violates the Kelvin–Planck statement: some heat must be rejected

items.text: Engine takes 1000 J, does 400 J of work, rejects 600 J to a cold reservoir
items.why: Allowed: η = 40% and heat is rejected

items.text: Heat flows by itself from a cold body to a hot body
items.why: Violates the Clausius statement

items.text: A refrigerator uses work to move heat from its cold inside to a warm room
items.why: Allowed: heat goes cold → hot only because work is done

items.text: Friction turns all the work done into heat
items.why: Allowed: the law forbids the reverse (all heat → work) as the sole result

items.text: Heat flows from hot tea to the cooler room
items.why: Natural direction of heat flow

items.text: An engine with 100% efficiency
items.why: No heat engine can turn all the absorbed heat into work

items.text: An engine between 500 K and 300 K with η = 50%
items.why: Even a Carnot engine there has η = 1 − 300/500 = 40%

p.challenge: Decide which of these could really happen.
A particle in SHM has amplitude 5 cm and period 2 s, and is at x = +5 cm at t = 0. Set A, ω = 2π/T and φ so that x = A cos(ωt + φ) sits on the dashed graph.
A body in SHM has A = 10 cm and ω = 5 rad s⁻¹. Set them and check v_max = ωA = 50 cm s⁻¹ at the mean position. Where is v zero, and where is |a| = ω²A largest?
A 1 kg block on a spring of k = 100 N m⁻¹. Since k = mω², set ω so the lab shows k = 100 N m⁻¹; the period should then be T = 2π√(m/k) ≈ 0.63 s.
m = 2 kg on a spring of k = 200 N m⁻¹ (ω = √(k/m) = 10 rad s⁻¹), amplitude 10 cm. Set A and ω so v_max = 100 cm s⁻¹. Watch KE and PE swap twice per cycle while E = ½kA² = 1 J stays fixed.
Set the string to 40 cm, press Start and time 10 oscillations. Is T close to 2π√(L/g) ≈ 1.27 s? Then double the length: does T double?
Make a seconds pendulum (T = 2 s, so each swing takes 1 s). Predict its length first from L = gT²/(4π²) with g = 9.8 m s⁻².
Watch the marked particle: it only bobs up and down while the crest, carrying energy, moves along — like a paper boat on ripples. Make the wave travel at 3 m s⁻¹: does the particle travel any faster?
In y = a sin(kx − ωt), the angular wave number is k = 2π/λ. Set the wave so that k = 4π ≈ 12.6 rad m⁻¹. What is λ? Then read ω = 2πν.
A 2 m wire of mass 0.04 kg has μ = 0.02 kg m⁻¹. Set μ and the tension T so a transverse wave travels at v = √(T/μ) = 50 m s⁻¹. Then change f: λ changes, but does v?
A girl shouts in front of a cliff and hears the echo after 2 s (v = 340 m s⁻¹). Sound goes there AND back, so d = vt/2. Set the distance and shout to check.
Phasors: two waves of amplitude 3 mm with phase difference φ add like vectors at angle φ. Drag the second phasor (keep it 3 mm) to φ = π/2 and read A = 2a cos(φ/2). Then try φ = 0 and φ = π.
Make a standing wave on a 1 m string (v = 100 m s⁻¹) whose adjacent nodes are 20 cm apart. Node spacing is λ/2, so λ = 40 cm. Which harmonic is it, and at what frequency?
A pipe 0.5 m long, closed at one end (v = 340 m s⁻¹): ν = (2n − 1)v/4L. Step through its modes and find the 3rd harmonic. Why is there no 2nd harmonic?
Resonance tube with a 500 Hz fork (v = 340 m s⁻¹, λ = 68 cm). The air column is 51 cm = 3λ/4. Tune the source to resonate at 500 Hz. Where was the first resonance (λ/4)? Note L₂ − L₁ = λ/2.
Fork A is 512 Hz. Tune fork B so you hear 5 beats per second: there are two answers. Loading B with wax lowers its frequency and the beats fall to 3 per second. Which answer is B?
